Frameworks for Evaluation
Contribution Mapping [62]
Tracks how people, organizations, and technologies contribute
to knowledge creation. It looks at relationships, shared learning,
and “alignment efforts” between partners. For example,
evaluators make maps and interview participants to trace how
ideas and collaborations evolve. 
SIAMPI (Social Impact Assessment through Productive
Interactions) [63]
 Measures “productive interactions” between researchers and
others, such as meetings, partnerships, shared publications, or
funding. The idea here is that social impact comes from these
interactions, not just final outputs. 
24

Flows of Knowledge [65]
Focuses on how knowledge and influence flow between
researchers, funders, policymakers, and communities.
Evaluators look at how relationships and awareness change,
not just formal results.
Social Effectiveness [66]
Looks at whether an intervention helps people understand each
other and build new social connections. It studies how
relationships and shared meaning develop as part of the
project
Intermediate Evaluation
Formative Evaluation [67]
 Provides ongoing feedback while a project is being implemented.
Uses interviews, reflections, and creative tools (like “rivers” or
“graffiti walls”) to help teams adapt in real time.
 
 Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) [68]
 Examines how new practices or interventions become part of
everyday routines. It looks at sense-making (coherence),
engagement (participation), doing the work (collective action), and
reflection (monitoring).
PROSECO [69]
 A co-creation–specific framework that evaluates five dimensions:
delivery, participation, experience, context, and impact. It’s flexible,
because users can mix and match components to suit their
evaluation goals.

COM-B Model [70]
 Used to understand and change behavior. It looks at whether
people have the Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation to act,

 A decision tool for evaluating whether an intervention is
Acceptable, Practical, Effective, Affordable, Safe, and

ASIRPA [72]
Traces how research leads to socio-economic impacts through

S&T Human Capital [73]
This approach to evaluation typically focuses on the researchers -

Integrated Evaluation
These frameworks connect multiple levels of evaluation. 

Realist Evaluation [75]
Asks, “What works, for whom, in what context, and why?” Instead of
linear cause-and-effect, it examines how social mechanisms work
differently in different settings, making it a good fit for complex co-
creation. 
Logic Models [76]
Simple visual tools linking project inputs →  activities →  outputs →
outcomes. They help clarify shared goals and assumptions by using a
diagrammatic model linking activities to objectives based on the
underlying change, and with reference to the theory behind the change
expected. Simply put, a logic model attempts to convey visually the
logic of the program (connection between program activities and the
program's desired outcomes). 
MRC Process Evaluation [77]
A health research framework that integrates design, implementation,
and outcomes. It balances structure with flexibility and emphasizes
feedback, fidelity, and learning across project stages.
PARiHS [78] [79]
Focuses on the interaction between Evidence, Context, and Facilitation
in implementing research. It values diverse forms of evidence (including
local knowledge) and sees implementation as a dynamic, negotiated
process.
 Institute for Work & Health (IWH) Research Impact Model [80]:
 This model offers a structured way to trace how research translates
into real-world outcomes by moving through three stages of impact:
immediate outputs (publications, briefs), intermediate outcomes:
(research uptake in policy, workplace practices), and final outcomes
(societal benefits – improved health and lower system costs). It
acknowledges that impact becomes more difficult the further one
moves from dissemination toward long-term societal change.

Mapping Assessment Paths in the AI Landscape 
Three waypoints for assessment design 
These waypoints offer a starting point for assessment design that works regardless of your 
position on AI — whether you are integrating it, restricting it, or building students’ critical 
literacy around it. Work through them before making AI-related decisions about any 
assessment, course, or program. 
 
Waypoint 1 — Purpose (of assessment) 
What is this assessment actually for? Rather than focussing on format or deliverable, 
consider the knowledge, process, judgment, or skill the assessment seeks to develop or 
measure. 
Question: What is the intellectual work required of the student? What is this assessment 
meant to reveal about the learning that has taken place? 
Waypoint 2 — Authenticity (of engagement) 
What does genuine student engagement look like here? This waypoint asks you to consider 
the authenticity of the learning process undertaken by the student as they are en route to the 
final “hand-in” version of the assessment. 
Question: What does authentic engagement with this assessment look like? What would 
superficial or substituted engagement look like by contrast? 
Waypoint 3 — Trust (in assessment) 
What does this assessment need to be trustworthy? Here we consider what is needed (or 
assumed) when we trust in our assessments. 
Question: What does this assessment need in order to be trustworthy? How can you make 
its trust-bearing elements stronger and more transparent? 
 
Once you have worked through these three waypoints, the AI question becomes more specific 
and more answerable: Does AI undermine what this assessment is actually for? Does it allow 
students to bypass genuine intellectual engagement? Does it threaten the design features this 
assessment depends on? 
 
 
  

Field notes: six questions for your practice 
A portable version of the three waypoints for independent reflection or 
collaborative use. Apply to any assessment, course, or program. 
 
Purpose (of assessment) 
– What is this assessment/course/program actually for, in one sentence? 
– What would still be worth assessing here if AI could handle everything else? 
 
Authenticity (of engagement) 
– What would it look like if a student genuinely grappled with this, and how is that different 
from producing a polished response? 
– What in the current design makes genuine engagement more likely than surface 
engagement? 
 
Trust (in assessment) 
– What is this assessment/course/program quietly assuming about how students engage? 
– Is that assumption earned by the design, or is it a hope?

The following are the AI disclosure statements I use for my research essay assignment in my first-
year English course (called ENGL 102: Analysis and Argument) and a literary research assignment 
in my English 103 course (Introduction to Literature) and also for a first-year writing course (called 
Writing 101) in which students write a personal reflection/theory of writing at the end of the course 
at MacEwan University.  
This is from page 2 of the assignment instructions, which I showed as an example in my breakout 
room during the Hack-a-Thon on April 14th and mentioned at the end of the session:  
You may use generative AI in this assignment, if you wish. Remember that when students do use 
generative AI in their assignments, they need to show where and how they have done so, or it could 
be considered academic dishonesty. See p. 6-7 of the course outline. You also need to ensure that 
your sources actually exist and are not fabricated, etc. Whether you use AI or not, you must choose 
one of the AI disclosure statements below to clearly explain how and to what extent you used AI in 
your essay. You must also use in-text citations and include generative AI in your works cited list if 
you used it in your essay. Please see the information on MLA.org for how to do 
so: https://style.mla.org/citing-generative-ai-updated-revised/ Assignments that do not include in-
text citations and a works cited list will receive a mark of zero.  
Choose one of the following generative AI disclosure statements and include it after your works 
cited (even if you did not use generative AI at all in your assignment):  
1) Generative AI such as ChatGPT, DALL.E 2, Grammarly AI, and Microsoft Copilot were not used in 
any way when drafting, writing, researching, or revising this assignment. The only tools used when 
writing this assignment were spelling and grammar check in Microsoft Word, Google Docs, and 
Grammarly.  
2) Generative AI such as ChatGPT, DALL.E 2, Grammarly AI, and Microsoft Copilot were only used in 
this assignment to suggest alternate wording, clarify sentence structure, and provide suggestions 
through predictive text. Tools used included [list the tools used here].  
3) Generative AI such as ChatGPT, DALL.E 2, Grammarly AI, and Microsoft Copilot were used in this 
assignment to generate an outline or first draft. It was also used to suggest alternate wording, 
clarify sentence structure, and provide suggestions through predictive text. Tools used included [list 
the tools used here]. All AI output was checked for accuracy and was only used to create a 
framework for the essay, which the author then fleshed out using examples from their own work and 
original research.  

4) Generative AI such as ChatGPT, DALL.E 2, Grammarly AI, and Microsoft Copilot were used 
substantially in this assignment to generate the essay and find sources for this assignment. It was 
also used to suggest alternate wording, clarify sentence structure, and provide suggestions through 
predictive text. Tools used included [list the tools used here]. All AI output was checked for 
accuracy, and the research results were thoroughly examined for quality and relevance. The author

Sample AI-Scaffolded Assignments Presented During the AI & 
Assessment Hack-a-Thon on Integrating AI Literacy into Assessment 
Practice at York University on April 14, 2026 
Dr. Susan Hesemeier 
Department of English 
MacEwan University 
Edmonton, Alberta 
hesemeiers@macewan.ca 
Over the past couple of years, I have created, tested, and refined a number of assignments in which 
AI use was explicitly allowed or required with proper documentation and reflection on the process.  
I teach mostly first-year English courses at MacEwan University in Edmonton, Alberta. First-year 
courses tended to be the ones in which high numbers of students were using generative AI without 
proper attribution, even when they were clearly not permitted to use generative AI according to the 
statements that were included in my course outline and assignment instructions.  
I started using “AI-scaffolded” assignments a couple of years ago after attending MacEwan 
University’s “AI Showcase: Your AI Teaching Journey/Early Explorations,” which was organized by the 
Centre for Teaching and Learning. In one of the sessions, a psychology professor (Dr. Kristine 
Peace) demonstrated an assignment in which she had students use generative AI to create a first 
draft of a presentation, and then students critiqued and evaluated the output from the generative AI 
using the comment captions in Word before creating the final presentation. I adapted this idea for 
essay assignments in English courses and then worked with an educational developer from 
MacEwan’s Centre for Teaching and Learning (Geneve Champoux) to hone the description of the 
steps, and she provided the link to the guide for creating prompts and ideas for the framework for 
evaluating the AI output in Step 2 in the example below. My innovations in assessment design were 
the result of collaboration and sharing ideas at MacEwan University, and I was happy to share them 
more broadly at York University’s Hack-a-Thon. 
In my AI-scaffolded essay assignments, students had to use generative AI to create a first draft or 
"Step 1" and then use the comments within Word to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the 
AI output (in "Step 2"). Then for a third step, they submitted the final comparison essay or rhetorical 
analysis essay, and if they did not want to use any of the AI output in the final step, they did not 
need to. For students who did not wish to use AI due to concerns with its environmental impact or 
other issues, I provided them with the option to use a draft that had already been generated in a 
previous term (so that no new output was being produced from an AI prompt, and so that they 
would still be able to do the review/evaluation of the AI output in Step 2).  
The following is one of the AI-scaffolded assignment examples I demonstrated in my breakout room 
during the Hack-a-Thon on April 14th and described to everyone at the end of the session. This is a 
comparison essay assignment I use in my first-year English course (English 103: Introduction to 
Literature), and I use similar assignments in other courses at MacEwan University (e.g., a rhetorical 
analysis essay in English 102: Analysis and Argument and Writing 101: First-Year Writing).  

English 103 Comparison Essay Assignment 
For this essay, you are required to use AI such as Microsoft Copilot or ChatGPT to generate a 
first draft of the essay. Microsoft Copilot is available to students for free by selecting Work or 
School Account and then logging in with your MacEwan ID and password 
at https://copilot.microsoft.com/. You will then use the comments in Word or Google Docs to mark 
up the AI output to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses in the AI-generated essay and clearly 
identify what could be improved in the essay. Then, you will revise the AI-generated essay. Please 
see the examples in the lecture notes folder. You do not need to use any of the AI-generated content 
in the essay you submit in Step 3 of this assignment, but if you do, you need to show where you have 
done so (using in-text citations after quotations and paraphrases from the AI-generated content, 
along with an entry in your works cited list). Please see the information about generative AI in the 
course outline and in the MLA’s guidelines on how to cite AI-generated 
content: https://style.mla.org/citing-generative-ai-updated-revised/ 
Here's a quick guide to creating prompts in Copilot that may be useful for Step 
1: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9b0LOSjq39w 
You will be submitting 3 documents: 
1) The initial results of the AI prompt (i.e., the AI-generated first draft of the essay), worth 10%; 
2) The marked-up AI-generated essay using the comments and reviewing tools in Word (see the 
example in the lecture notes folder), worth 20%; 
* Note that if you use Google Docs, you will need to download your file as a Word document (not a 
PDF) to save your comments; if you use Word, you can save it as either a Word document or PDF. 
3) The revised/rewritten essay based on the revisions to the Microsoft Copilot or ChatGPT output, 
worth 70%. Assignments that only include the initial results of the Microsoft Copilot or ChatGPT 
prompt (i.e., the AI-generated first draft of the essay) will be limited to 10%. If the revised essay in 
Step 3 does not have in-text citations with page numbers and a works cited list for all sources, 
including any use of generative AI in Step 3, it will receive a zero. 
Framework for Step 2: Evaluating the AI Output 
In considering the strengths and weaknesses of the AI output from Step 1, consider the following:  
 
a) Depth of analysis: Has the program picked out elements of the story, novel, or poem that 
provide the best examples? Is it specific about how these elements reflect the chosen theme? 
Does it make thoughtful observations about the significance of these themes or elements, or 
does it provide only general or surface-level analysis? 
b) Accuracy and sufficiency of sources: Do the citations provided by the AI exist? Has the AI 
represented what those sources said accurately? Are these high-quality, scholarly sources, or 
are there better sources available in the library’s database? Is there enough citation provided, 
or are there claims being made that should be backed up by your primary sources? Remember 
that in the final essay you submit in Step 3, you should not have any secondary sources such 
as articles and book chapters about the literary works (i.e., you should only be using evidence 
from your primary sources), so if the AI output has included information from any sources other 
than the short story, novel, or poem you are writing about, you should take that out. 

c) Quality of writing: AI programs generally produce writing with accurate grammar and 
punctuation, but good writing is about more than correctness. Is the tone scholarly? Does it 
sound like it was written by a machine? Is it composed like an essay with a compelling 
introduction, good transitions, and flow, or does it read like a series of answers strung 
together? What revisions may be needed to make the paper sound more human or more 
academic?   
 
Framework/Rubric for Step 3: The Revised AI Output/Final Draft of the Comparison Essay  
[I also provide a rubric that I use to assess the content/development, structure/organization, 
grammar/punctuation, and documentation/format, but I have taken that out for brevity here: I 
demonstrated it within the AI Hack-a-Thon, along with examples of Steps 1-3, and I am happy to 
share those by email or meeting through Teams, Zoom, etc.]  
 
I also have a research essay assignment in which students can optionally use generative AI, but 
with in-text citations after any quotations and paraphrases from AI content, along with an entry in a 
works cited list, and they must choose from four levels of AI disclosure statements I developed, 
even if they did not use generative AI at all. These disclosure statements range from no AI use to 
extensive AI use with review and revision of the output along with disclosure of the tools that were 
used. I also showed these statements as examples during the AI Hack-a-Thon. 
In addition to AI-scaffolded assignments and AI disclosure statements, I have also implemented 
various strategies to limit or restrict AI use in assessments. i.e., I allow students to use generative AI 
in only two assessments per term, in the way I have described for the two assignments above. All 
other AI use is prohibited, and I either have students complete written assignments in class or 
through presentations and discussions in class, along with smaller participation-based 
assignments that are marked for completion and that help students prepare for the final exam 
(which is written in class, not open book, and worth 30% of their mark). These redesigns intend to 
reduce AI use or make learning more about completing the activity (and seeing students participate 
in the activity) rather than just assessing the outcome/finished product. I also use staged drafts, 
group collaborative writing assignments, writing process reflections, peer review, and other 
activities. 
What I've learned from the changes I've made in my assessments is that even if AI is now available 
for students to use in almost every tool they will encounter (whether it is Google, Grammarly, 
Microsoft Word, etc.), they can learn how to use it in a way that does not pose academic integrity 
issues, if they choose to use it, by disclosing how and to what extent they have done so (similar to 
when students use ideas or wording from a source). They can also become aware of its weaknesses 
and strengths by learning how to critique and evaluate AI-generated content. By making these 
changes in my assessments over the past couple of years, and in consultation with educational 
developers at MacEwan's Centre for Teaching and Learning, I have created assessments that can 
teach students critical AI literacy while circumventing the academic integrity office. 
If I were to adapt my AI-scaffolded comparison essay assignment for my upcoming classes, I might 
combine Steps 1 and 2 (although I do like that dividing this into two steps creates a clear separation 

between what is raw AI output, what is the student’s evaluation of the AI output, and what is their 
own work, with any use of the AI-generated content properly attributed in Step 3). I would also have 
students include one of the AI disclosure statements I use for my research assignments (although I 
usually do the AI-scaffolded comparison essay assignment before the research essay, so keeping it 
simple—by stating that if they haven’t included AI in their works cited list in Step 3, that means they 
didn’t use it in that step—works well for this assignment because I can also see the raw AI output in 
their Step 1).  
Some people have wondered if it takes extra time to mark a scaffolded assignment that has an extra 
couple of steps (rather than just the Step 3 comparison essay), but since I mark the first couple of 
steps for completion or the level of detail included in their evaluation of the AI output in Step 2, it 
does not take a lot of time to mark the first two steps, and I end up spending around the same 
amount of time marking the assignment as I would for a non-scaffolded comparison essay. It is 
similar to an assignment in which instructors might have students submit their notes, drafts, and 
classmates’ peer reviews of early versions of their assignments, instead of just submitting the final 
copy of the essay, so that instructors can see their writing process and development of the essay, 
rather than just the finished product (the only difference is that I have students use generative AI to 
create the first draft—since many students are doing this anyway, whether they were permitted to 
or not, and without attributing it—and having students submit the assignment in these three steps 
puts transparency back into the writing process and shows them how to properly document or 
disclose where they had used any content from generative AI in the final essay). 
I am happy to receive any feedback on this assignment, which is in part why I wanted to 
demonstrate these examples during the Hack-a-Thon at York University’s AI Intensive (and due to 
the uniqueness of Step 2 with using Word to add comments/review the output, it does work better 
to demonstrate this assignment visually and verbally rather than just in writing, so I can also meet 
via Zoom or Teams if anyone who wasn’t in the session would like to see these examples). I would 
also be delighted to see ways in which you would suggest adapting these AI-scaffolded 
assignments or examples of how you have adjusted them for your courses. 
Thank you to all the organizers of York University’s AI Intensive for this great opportunity to share 
resources, receive feedback on our assessment innovations, and both lead and learn from other 
educators regarding AI and assessment! 
All the best,

Academic Integrity and Generative Artificial Intelligence Technology 
 
The purpose of this document is to communicate and clarify the policy guidelines 
regarding the use of AI technology for academic work. It is not a policy document. For 
more information about York’s expectations for academic honesty, please refer to 
York’s Senate Policy on Academic Honesty. 
 
New artificial intelligence (AI) tools are generating much discussion within higher 
education because of their high level of sophistication and human-like abilities to 
research, write, problem-solve, create art, produce videos, and even to evolve. There is 
concern that use of generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, GPT-3, and DALL-E) will 
make it easier or more tempting for students to engage in academic misconduct and 
will jeopardize academic integrity efforts at the institution.  
 
To promote clear and consistent practices, students across York are not authorized to 
use text-, image-, code-, or video-generating AI tools when completing their academic 
work unless explicitly permitted by a specific instructor in a particular course. 
Otherwise, using AI tools to aid in academic work (in whole or part) that is submitted 
for credit constitutes one or more breaches under York’s Senate Policy on Academic 
Honesty (“Senate Policy”). 
 
Specifically, their use could be considered to be cheating, which is defined as “the 
attempt to gain an improper advantage in an academic evaluation” (Senate Policy, 
section 2.1.1). Associate Deans who are involved in enforcing Academic Honesty at 
York can consider how different types of unauthorized student use of AI technology 
are already captured in the non-exhaustive list of “cheating” examples currently 
offered in the Senate Guidelines under the Senate Policy: for instance, “obtaining 
assistance by means of documentary, electronic or other aids which are not approved 
by the instructor” (Senate Policy, section 2.1.1). 
 
Additionally, the unauthorized use of AI tools (such as image-generating AI, like DALL-
E) could be considered to be plagiarism. Plagiarism occurs when another’s work is 
presented as one’s own without proper attribution, including “another’s artistic or 
technical work or creation” (Senate Policy, section 2.1.3).  
 
Instructors are encouraged to discuss these AI tools with their students and to clarify 
what their expectations are for their use. If the use of such tools is to be authorized in
